explanation:
The grid always has one **wall**: a full line of a single colour (colour 2 here) along one border. In pair 1 it is the left column, in pair 2 the bottom row, and in pair 3 the right column. Every other object is a two-cell domino.

**What changes.** In the output each domino slides straight toward the wall as a rigid piece. It stops when it touches the wall or a domino that has already stopped, like Tetris gravity aimed at the wall.

**Checking this by hand on pair 1 (wall on the left):**
- 3 at x=3–4 slides to x=1–2.
- 4 at x=7–8 is stopped by 3, so it ends at x=3–4.
- The vertical 5 (rows 1–2) slides to x=1.
- 6 in row 2 is stopped by 5, so it ends at x=2–3.
- 7 in row 4 slides to x=1–2.
- The vertical 8 (rows 3–4) is stopped by 7 in row 4, so it ends at x=3.

All six positions match the output.

**Pairs 2 and 3.** I also checked them by hand. In pair 2 (wall at the bottom), 4 rests on 5, and 8 and 6 both end up stacked against 4. In pair 3 (wall on the right), 5 stops against 6, and 9 stops against 8. The program below has not been run against the train pairs yet, so these hand checks are the only verification so far.

**Construction.**
1. Locate the wall: a full line of one non-background colour lying on a border. This gives the fall direction.
2. Take the other objects as 4-connected components and sort them by their distance to the wall, nearest first.
3. Drop each object one step at a time until the next cell is blocked or off the grid. Objects nearer the wall have already settled, so each later object stops on them correctly.
4. Emit the canvas after each object lands.

**On the test input**, the wall is the top row. The dominoes rise in order of how close they are to row 0 and stack upward against the wall and each other. Same-coloured dominoes are not adjacent to each other, so each one stays its own component.
